In 1958, Challen et al. conducted a study on a confectionery firm in England that manufactured medicinal lozenges. 14. Workers began complaining in 1950 about the chloroform vapor released during the production of the lozenges. 15. A part-time work system was introduced to address complaints of lassitude, flatulence, dyspepsia symptoms (e.g., water brash), dry mouth, thirst, depression, irritability, and frequent painful urination. 16. In 1954, a new team of operators was hired, and in 1955, an exhaust ventilation system was installed, allowing work to proceed without further interruptions. 17. 18. 19. Air samples were collected continuously in the breathing zone of the operator during a 20-minute ingredient mixing process, with sampling conducted at a rate of 2 liters per minute using silica gel-filled U-tubes. 20. A 6-liter grab sample was taken at a point in the operation where peak concentrations were expected. 21. Additional 30-minute air samples were collected in the breathing zones of cutting room operators during two production periods under current conditions and three periods under simulated conditions. 22. Clinical investigations were performed on three groups of workers. 23. 24. These workers, exposed to chloroform vapor at concentrations likely ranging from 77 to 237 ppm, were observed staggering in the work area. 25. 26. A second group, termed short service operators, consisted of nine employees who replaced the long service operators. 27. 28. Among the remaining seven, five reported dryness of the mouth and throat at work, two experienced lassitude in the evening, one complained of lassitude and flatulence at work, and two had experiences similar to those of the long service operators. 29. The short service operators worked in areas where chloroform concentrations ranged from 23 to 71 ppm. 30. A third group of five employees, who worked in other departments of the firm, served as controls and exhibited no symptoms. 31. Tests of liver function (e.g., thymol turbidity, thymol flocculation, direct van den Bergh, and serum bilirubin), clinical examinations, and urinary urobilinogen levels showed no significant differences among the three groups of workers. 32. Of these, 68 were exposed to chloroform for 1–4 years and continued to have contact with it, 39 had previous contact with chloroform, 23 had a history of viral hepatitis with jaundice 2–3 years earlier and were designated as post-icterus controls, and 165 worked in a germ-free area with no history of viral hepatitis. 34. 35. A complete medical history was taken, and 60 individuals were hospitalized for determination of BSP clearance and urinary urobilinogen levels. 36. Air samples from the production room were analyzed for chloroform concentrations using the Grabowicz method, with levels ranging from 2 to 205 ppm. 37. 38. The authors compared the frequency of viral hepatitis and jaundice among city inhabitants aged 18 and older with that of the 68 pharmaceutical workers exposed to chloroform. 39. In 1960, 0.35% of city inhabitants had viral hepatitis, compared to 16.67% of chloroform-exposed workers. 40. In 1961, the frequency was 0.22% for city inhabitants and 7.50% for chloroform workers. 41. In 1962, the frequency of viral hepatitis was 0.38% for city inhabitants and 4.4% for chloroform workers. 42. However, they did not provide data on the incidence of viral hepatitis among other plant workers, which could have clarified questions about sanitary practices and facilities in the plant. 43. Most workers exposed to chloroform during the investigation period reported symptoms such as headache, nausea, belching, and loss of appetite. 44. Among the 68 workers using chloroform, 10 cases of splenomegaly were identified, compared to none in the control group. 45. The authors did not explain the splenomegaly but noted its absence in the control group.
